conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had this sharp pain in my lower left side for a few days now. It’s the same kind of pain I’ve had before with my endometriosis—comes in waves and shoots down into my rectum and left leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And has it been worse than usual? Did you have your period?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m not on my period. It’s just as bad as last time—maybe worse. I’ve tried all my usual meds: tramadol, gabapentin, the lidocaine patch, even the vaginal diazepam. Nothing’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve thrown up twice. I feel nauseous all day. No fevers or urinary symptoms, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll check your vitals and get some labs. You had a CT scan in the ER earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they did a CT of my belly and pelvis. I was hoping it would show something, but they said it was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The report confirms no acute issues—no appendicitis, no kidney stones blocking anything, no bowel problems. But there are tiny calcifications in both kidneys, less than 2 mm. They’re not blocking anything, so likely not causing your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history and the fact that the imaging is clear, it’s likely related to your endometriosis. The pain pattern matches what you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had two hospital visits in the past week for this. It’s really affecting my work and daily life.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re admitting you—to focus on better pain control and adjust your treatment plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was tachycardic in the ER and I’m nauseous—should I get IV fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable now. You’re tolerating fluids by mouth, so we don’t think you need an IV line. We’ll keep an eye on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I asked for a central line before, but they said no. I just want to make sure I can get meds quickly if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that. But since you’re not on IV meds and can take things by mouth, a central line isn’t necessary and carries risks. We’ll manage your pain with oral meds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs came back—everything looks stable. No infection, your kidney function is good, and your lithium level is in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My mood’s been okay—I’ve been taking my lithium and trazodone like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep those going. For your pain, we’re starting a new medication called indomethacin—25 mg three times a day. It’s a non-narcotic anti-inflammatory that may help with endometriosis-related pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidneys? I saw something about kidney stones on the CT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. The stones are tiny and not blocking anything. But we’ll monitor your kidney function with a blood test in a week or two, just to be safe while you’re on this med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team came by to see you. They recommend increasing your gabapentin to 600 mg four times a day and your tizanidine to 4 mg three times a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s higher than I’ve taken before. Will it make me sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might at first. We’ll start the new doses tomorrow and monitor how you feel. The goal is better pain control without narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ve been trying to avoid increasing opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now? Any change since starting indomethacin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still pretty bad, but maybe a little less sharp. I’m still nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you something for nausea. And we’ll keep adjusting the pain meds. You’re also still on your omeprazole, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take omeprazole daily for reflux. Please don’t stop it—indomethacin can irritate the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re already on it, so that’s perfect. We’ll keep it going to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain seems a bit better today, and your vitals are stable. We’re planning to discharge you later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I still have pain, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s manageable with the new meds, and there’s no sign of a surgical issue. The plan is to continue the indomethacin for two weeks, increase your gabapentin and tizanidine, and follow up with the pain clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a waiting list for pelvic floor therapy. Can they move my appointment up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team is already working on that. They’ll try to get you in sooner. Call their office in a week if you haven’t heard anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Lupron shot? My next one is due soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your next dose is due soon. Make sure you get that from your OB/GYN as scheduled. It’s part of your long-term endometriosis management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Take the indomethacin for two weeks, increase your gabapentin and tizanidine as discussed, and keep all your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER if you have fevers, vomiting, chest pain, or worsening pain. Otherwise, call your pain clinic or OB/GYN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up and take the meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing by staying on top of this. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.
